briefingMeta.abstract_html:
HMTc applies selected infant-food contaminant benchmarks to supplements as voluntary program criteria. Concentration, serving size, preparation and body weight all matter to exposure. The reviewed sources do not establish that all supplement rules assume adults or that adult products are appropriate for children.

This briefing distinguishes the original food categories from HMTc's supplement criteria and explains why concentration limits must be read alongside product scope, preparation and intended use.

references.title: USP General Chapter <2232>: Elemental Contaminants in Dietary Supplements
references.meta_html: United States Pharmacopeia. General Chapter <2232>, USP–NF (2022), public publisher preview. Scope: finished dosage forms labeled as conforming to USP or NF. Subscription numerical tables and their derivation were not reviewed.

references.title: Thailand MOPH Notification No. 414 (2020) — Standards for Contaminants in Food
references.meta_html: Ministry of Public Health, 20 March 2020; Government Gazette, 20 May 2020. Annex 1 lead row: food supplements 1 mg/kg as prepared for consumption. Officially hosted unofficial English translation; Thai text controls. Replaces the former unverified four-jurisdiction grouping.

references.title: ASEAN and Singapore health-supplement contaminant guidelines
references.meta_html: ASEAN Guidelines on Limits of Contaminants for Health Supplements, version 2.0 (June 2015), and Singapore HSA Health supplements overview (accessed September 2026). Both list lead 10 ppm; legal status and target-user safety requirements require separate attention.

references.title: Proposition 65 Safe Harbor Levels — Maximum Allowable Dose Levels
references.meta_html: California OEHHA: lead MADL 0.5 µg/day. Daily-exposure safe harbor under Proposition 65; not a food concentration limit or general child-safety guarantee.

references.title: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food
references.meta_html: European Commission (2023), Annex I. Cadmium 5 µg/kg applies to specified liquid formula made from cow-milk proteins or protein hydrolysates; inorganic arsenic 10 µg/kg applies to liquid formula. Powder and soy categories differ.

references.title: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in food
references.meta_html: European Commission (2024). Nickel maximum 100 µg/kg for liquid formula as marketed; powder maxima differ. These are formula requirements, not legal supplement limits.

references.title: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, Standard 1.4.1 — Contaminants and Natural Toxicants
references.meta_html: FSANZ. Standard 1.4.1; Schedule 19 compilation of 13 September 2024 and amendment F2024L01151. Formula lead 10 µg/kg; aluminium 500 µg/kg for specified formula, 1000 for soy and 200 for preterm special-medical products. Preparation and transition provisions apply.

references.title: Update of the Risk Assessment of Nickel in Food and Drinking Water
references.meta_html: EFSA CONTAM Panel. EFSA Journal 2020;18(11):6268. Chronic TDI 13 µg Ni/kg body weight/day. High-percentile exposures exceed it in many young groups; mean exposure was generally below or near it. Total-diet assessment, not a supplement concentration limit.

briefingFeatured.claim: HMTc applies selected infant-food contaminant benchmarks to supplements as voluntary criteria. The comparison must state the product and exposure basis; meeting those criteria does not establish that an adult supplement is suitable for a child.
